title: The Complaint Detective
description: Mento needs your help. The colony is full of complaints, and every complaint is a clue. Listen, dig with the Five WHYs, run the PAIN/SIZE/GAP test, and pitch your idea — can you turn a complaint into a real business?
theme: Turning everyday complaints into business ideas — the culmination of the Mento Entrepreneurship Workshop.
learning_objectives: Hear complaints as hidden business opportunities
Apply the Five WHYs to dig past surface problems
Run the PAIN, SIZE, and GAP tests on an idea
Deliver a 60-second pitch with the 5-part formula
learning_concept: Great entrepreneurs don't invent problems — they listen for them. Every complaint is a clue, and the deeper you dig, the bigger the opportunity.
psychological_framework: Design Thinking (IDEO) + Effectuation (Sarasvathy) — empathize, define, ideate, prototype, pitch.
coaching_moment: You don't need a genius idea. You need a real problem and the patience to ask WHY five times before jumping to a solution.

story_intro.intro_narrative: It's a quiet Saturday in your colony. Mento taps your shoulder: 'You hear that grumbling? That's not noise — that's data. Every complaint is a clue. Walk with me. Some of these voices might be hiding the next big idea.'

scenes.title: Aunty at the Market
scenes.narrative: Mento walks past the colony market. Sharma Aunty is pushing through a 30-minute queue at the vegetable shop. She huffs: 'Every single day, I waste an hour standing here. Why can't anyone just figure this out?' Mento's map starts glowing.
scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon Pixar-style. Indian residential colony market in the morning. A frustrated middle-aged woman in a saree stands in a long queue at a vegetable stall, looking at her watch. The Mento mascot (a friendly explorer with a glowing scroll) stands nearby listening. Warm sunlight, friendly atmosphere.

choices.label: Pull out a notebook and write the complaint down word for word.
choices.feedback: Yes! Mento writes: 'queue too long → pre-order app?' That's a clue, not a complaint.

choices.label: Tell Aunty to just shop online instead.
choices.feedback: Mento winces. You jumped to a solution before listening. Aunty walks off — and so does the clue.

choices.label: Ask Aunty: 'How often does this happen, and how much would you pay to skip the queue?'
choices.feedback: Mento's eyes go wide — you're not just listening, you're testing the PAIN level. That's how real entrepreneurs think.

scenes.title: Grocery Bag Trouble
scenes.narrative: Outside the market, Uncle Verma is wrestling four heavy grocery bags up the stairs of his building. He grumbles: 'No lift, no help, every single time my back hurts for two days.' Mento glances at you.
scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon Pixar-style. An elderly Indian man struggling up stairs of a residential building with heavy plastic grocery bags. Mento (friendly explorer mascot) watches with a glowing notebook. Soft afternoon light, tiled stairwell.

choices.label: Ignore it — back pain isn't a business idea.
choices.feedback: Mento shakes his head. Most great companies started with someone's back pain.

choices.label: Note it as a possible 'door-to-door grocery helper' service idea.
choices.feedback: Good clue collected! Now ask: how many uncles in this colony? In this city? That's your SIZE test.

choices.label: Stop and help Uncle carry the bags up.
choices.feedback: First the human, then the business. Mento smiles. Now you have empathy AND a clue.

scenes.title: Diya's Mother Loses Her Keys
scenes.narrative: Diya runs up: 'Mento! My mother loses her keys EVERY week. I want to invent unbreakable keys!' Mento raises an eyebrow. 'Diya... before we invent anything — let's ask WHY five times.'
scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon Pixar-style. A 12-year-old Indian girl named Diya excitedly showing a bunch of keys to Mento mascot. Mento holds a glowing scroll labeled '5 WHYs'. Bright living room with a wooden door visible.

choices.label: Skip the WHYs — start designing 'unbreakable keys' now.
choices.feedback: You fell in love with the solution. Mento groans. Most products that fail do exactly this.

choices.label: Ask WHY #1: Why does she lose them?
choices.feedback: Right! 'Because they fall loose in her handbag.' That's WHY #1. Four more to go.

choices.label: Ask Diya how her mother actually feels about losing them.
choices.feedback: 'She feels stupid and frustrated.' Mento nods — emotion is data. The pain is real.

scenes.title: The Real Problem
scenes.narrative: After 5 WHYs, you've dug from 'lost keys' all the way down to: 'Most handbags are just empty bags — designed with zero thought for what working women actually need every day.' Mento grins. THIS is a real business.
scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon Pixar-style. Mento mascot pointing at a glowing scroll showing a tree of 5 WHY questions branching downward, with a treasure-chest icon at the bottom labelled 'REAL PROBLEM'. Bright, magical atmosphere.

choices.label: Stick with 'unbreakable keys' anyway.
choices.feedback: Mento sighs. Resilience means changing your mind when the data tells you to.

choices.label: Pivot to 'smart organiser handbags for working professionals'.
choices.feedback: Massive pivot. Now your market just went from 'one mom' to 'every working woman in India'. That's the power of WHY.

choices.label: Talk to 5 more women before deciding.
choices.feedback: The careful path. Mento approves: real founders don't bet on one data point.

scenes.title: PAIN, SIZE, GAP
scenes.narrative: Mento's scroll lights up with three glowing icons. 'Before you build anything, run the three tests. PAIN: does it hurt enough? SIZE: how many people? GAP: is anyone solving this — badly?' Diya is ready. Pick which test matters most for the smart-handbag idea.
scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon Pixar-style. Mento mascot with a magical scroll showing three glowing test tubes labelled PAIN (red), SIZE (blue), GAP (green). Diya stands with a notebook ready to take notes. Whimsical lab background.

choices.label: PAIN test — interview 10 women, ask 'how much does this frustrate you 1-10?'
choices.feedback: Smart. If average is 8/10, you have a real business. If 3/10, save your time.

choices.label: SIZE test — count how many working women in India would buy a smart handbag.
choices.feedback: Investor-grade thinking. ~150 million working women in India. Even 0.1% = 150,000 customers.

choices.label: GAP test — visit 5 handbag stores, see who's already solving this.
choices.feedback: Field research! You discover most 'organiser bags' on the market are ugly and overpriced. That's your gap.

scenes.title: Meet Your Customer
scenes.narrative: Mento says: 'Don't build for everyone. Build for ONE person, vividly.' He hands you a card. 'Describe the one woman who would buy your bag tomorrow.' Pick the customer profile you want to design for.
scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon Pixar-style. Mento mascot holding three customer cards floating in mid-air, each showing a different Indian woman: a young teacher, a corporate professional, a doctor. Sticky notes and pencils around. Warm friendly studio.

choices.label: Anjali, 32, school teacher in Pune. Carries lesson plans, lunchbox, keys, phone. Hates clutter.
choices.feedback: Specific. Memorable. Buyable. This is a real customer.

choices.label: All working women in India aged 25-50.
choices.feedback: Too broad. When you design for everyone, nobody falls in love with it.

choices.label: Dr Priya, 38, paediatrician in Bengaluru. Always running between hospital and home, drops things.
choices.feedback: Sharp. A doctor's day is brutal — solving for her solves for many.

scenes.title: The 60-Second Pitch
scenes.narrative: An investor walks into the colony coffee shop. You have 60 seconds. Mento whispers: 'Problem. Solution. Who. Why-different. Ask.' Pick the pitch that gets the cheque.
scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon Pixar-style. A young entrepreneur (the player) standing at a small coffee shop table pitching to an investor in a suit. Mento mascot stands behind cheering with a stopwatch glowing 60 seconds. Warm cafe atmosphere with steam from coffee.

choices.label: 'I'm building the next big bag company. We'll be huge. Invest 1 crore.'
choices.feedback: Investor walks out. No problem stated, no customer named, no humility. Mento covers his face.

choices.label: 'Every working woman in India loses 10 minutes a day digging in her bag. I built Anjali — a smart organiser bag. Specifically for school teachers like Anjali, 32. Unlike fashion bags, mine has 7 dedicated compartments. I'm raising ₹15 lakh to manufacture the first 1000 units.'
choices.feedback: Investor leans forward. Real problem. Real customer. Real ask. THIS is a pitch. Mento beams.

choices.label: 'I noticed my friend's mother loses her keys. So I started asking why. Five whys later I found that 80% of working women lose 10+ minutes a day in their bags. I built a smart bag for women like Dr Priya. I need a co-founder more than money.'
choices.feedback: Honest, story-driven, asking for help over money. The investor offers BOTH money AND a co-founder intro. Mento applauds.

glossary_terms.definition: Asking 'does this problem hurt enough that someone will pay to fix it?'
Asking 'how many people share this exact problem?'
Asking 'is anyone solving this — and badly enough that I can do 10x better?'
Asking WHY five times in a row to dig past a surface complaint to the real root problem.
A short, vivid description of one specific person who has the problem you want to solve.
A 60-second story explaining the problem, your solution, who it helps, and what you need to build it.

chapters.title: The Colony Walk
chapters.teaser: Mento is on a walk. Every voice is a possible business. Can you hear them?

chapters.title: Dig Deeper
chapters.teaser: Don't fall for the surface story. Ask WHY — five times.

chapters.title: Test the Idea
chapters.teaser: PAIN, SIZE, GAP — does your idea pass all three?

chapters.title: The Pitch
chapters.teaser: 60 seconds. One investor. Make it count.

rejected.title: Pitch Rejected
rejected.summary: The investor walked out. Why? Because you skipped the work — no real problem, no real customer, just hype. The good news: every great founder gets rejected. The bad news: you don't get a cheque without doing the homework first.
skill_summary: Try again — listen first, pitch last.

funded.title: Funded! ₹15 Lakh Cheque
funded.summary: Your pitch had everything: a real problem, a specific customer, a clear difference, and a precise ask. The investor signed. You're in business — and you got there by listening, digging, and testing.
skill_summary: You named one customer, not all customers.
You made an ask, not a beg.

funded_plus.title: Funded + Co-founder Intro
funded_plus.summary: The investor saw a founder who built a story from empathy, used data to back it up, and was humble enough to ask for help. That's rare. You got money AND a co-founder — the two hardest things to find.
skill_summary: Asking for help is strength, not weakness.
Real founders share credit before they share equity.

reflection_prompt: Of the 5 WHYs, the PAIN/SIZE/GAP test, and the customer profile — which one was the hardest for you? Why?
post_game_takeaways: Fall in love with the problem, not the solution.
One vivid customer beats a thousand vague ones.
A pitch without a problem is just noise.
